title: Endometrial Cancer
subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: Endometrial cancer is the commonest gynecologic malignancy in post‑menopausal women, presenting with abnormal uterine bleeding. Diagnosis relies on tissue sampling and staging guides surgery, radiotherapy and systemic therapy.

sections.p: A malignant tumour arising from the endometrial lining, most often an endometrioid adenocarcinoma. Diagnosis requires histologic confirmation from endometrial sampling.
b: Histology shows glandular proliferation with atypia; grade 1‑3 based on architecture and nuclear atypia
Immunohistochemistry (p53, mismatch repair proteins) helps identify Lynch syndrome

sections.p: Staging follows the FIGO 2023 surgical system, based on depth of myometrial invasion, cervical spread, nodal involvement and distant metastases.
b: Stage I: confined to uterus (IA ≤50% myometrium, IB >50%)
Stage II: cervical stromal invasion
Stage III: local spread to serosa, adnexa or nodes
Stage IV: bladder/rectal invasion or distant metastasis

sections.p: Risk factors are grouped into hormonal, genetic and environmental categories, with obesity and unopposed estrogen being the strongest.
b: Obesity (BMI ≥ 30) → peripheral aromatization of androgens
Nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause
Tamoxifen use, estrogen‑only HRT
Lynch syndrome (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 mutations)
Chronic anovulation (PCOS)
Diabetes, hypertension – common in East Africa

sections.p: The classic presentation is post‑menopausal bleeding, but pre‑menopausal women may have abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) or intermenstrual spotting.
b: Bleeding that is new, persistent, or heavier than usual
Pelvic pain is uncommon unless advanced disease
Weight loss, fatigue in late stages

t.b: Is the endometrium thickened? – Endometrial thickness ≥5 mm in post‑menopausal women suggests pathology; thin endometrium (<5 mm) makes cancer unlikely.
What is the histology? – Provides definitive diagnosis and grade; if unavailable, refer for hysterectomy specimen.
How deep is myometrial invasion? – High‑resolution MRI predicts IA vs IB and cervical involvement; if MRI not available, use intra‑operative assessment.
Is there distant spread? – Detects nodal or organ metastases; if CT unavailable, chest X‑ray and abdominal ultrasound are alternatives.

t.a: Molecular testing (MMR IHC or MSI PCR)
t.b: Is there Lynch syndrome? – Guides surveillance and immunotherapy; if not possible, refer for genetic counseling based on family history.

sections.p: Complications arise from local invasion or metastasis and can be life‑threatening.
b: Rapidly increasing bleeding causing anemia
Ureteric obstruction → hydronephrosis
Vaginal fistula from extensive disease
Pulmonary or hepatic metastases causing organ failure

sections.p: Treatment is stage‑directed, combining surgery, radiotherapy and systemic therapy. In low‑resource settings, surgery remains the cornerstone.
b: Stage I‑II: Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo‑oophorectomy; sentinel node biopsy if feasible.
Adjuvant radiotherapy (vaginal brachytherapy) for high‑grade or deep invasion.
Stage III‑IV: Consider combined external beam radiotherapy and chemotherapy (carboplatin + paclitaxel).
Hormone therapy (progestins) for selected low‑grade, fertility‑preserving patients.
Immunotherapy (PD‑1 inhibitors) for mismatch‑repair deficient tumours when available.

sections.p: Surveillance aims to detect recurrence early and manage long‑term risks.
b: Clinical exam and symptom review every 3‑6 months for 2 years, then annually.
Ultrasound or CT if symptoms recur.
Weight control, regular physical activity, and managing diabetes reduce future risk.
For Lynch syndrome carriers: annual colonoscopy and consider risk‑reducing hysterectomy after childbearing.

sections.p: Conditions that also cause abnormal uterine bleeding.
b: Endometrial hyperplasia – benign proliferation, may progress to cancer.
Uterine polyps – focal lesions, usually benign.
Adenomyosis – diffuse endometrial tissue within myometrium, causes heavy bleeding.

sections.p: Certain investigations may give false reassurance.
b: Thin endometrium on ultrasound can miss focal cancer; always sample if bleeding persists.
Normal CA‑125 does not exclude disease; it is not a screening test.
MRI may underestimate superficial cervical invasion; intra‑operative assessment remains gold standard.

whenToSeekHelp: Heavy or sudden uterine bleeding causing dizziness or fainting
Rapidly worsening pelvic pain with fever
Signs of urinary obstruction (flank pain, decreased urine output)

faq.q: Why is obesity such a strong risk factor?
faq.a: Adipose tissue converts androgens to estrogen, creating unopposed estrogen stimulation of the endometrium.

faq.q: Can a young woman get endometrial cancer?
faq.a: Yes, especially with Lynch syndrome, tamoxifen exposure, or chronic anovulation.

faq.q: Is a normal ultrasound enough to rule out cancer?
faq.a: No; persistent bleeding always requires histologic sampling regardless of ultrasound thickness.

exam: What history points differentiate endometrial cancer from benign AUB? — Emphasise post‑menopausal bleeding, risk factors (obesity, tamoxifen, Lynch), and duration of symptoms.

How would you manage a 62‑year‑old with post‑menopausal bleeding in a district hospital lacking MRI? — Perform pipelle biopsy; if cancer confirmed, arrange referral for hysterectomy; use ultrasound thickness to triage urgency.

Explain the FIGO stage IIA versus IIB distinction and its impact on treatment. — IIA: cervical stromal invasion without parametrial spread (surgery ± brachytherapy); IIB: parametrial involvement (requires radiotherapy).
Why is progestin therapy only suitable for selected patients? — It works for low‑grade, early‑stage disease in women desiring fertility; ineffective for high‑grade or deep invasion.
When is immunotherapy indicated in endometrial cancer? — In metastatic or recurrent tumors with mismatch‑repair deficiency or high microsatellite instability, after standard chemo.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral? — Sudden massive bleeding causing hemodynamic instability or new onset flank pain suggesting ureteric obstruction.
How does Lynch syndrome alter long‑term management? — Requires lifelong colonoscopic surveillance, consider risk‑reducing hysterectomy, and informs family testing.
What are the pitfalls of relying on CA‑125 in endometrial cancer? — It is not specific; normal levels do not exclude disease, and elevated levels may reflect other gynecologic conditions.
